newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss gunman shot priest for bothering him.
newsitem.headline: Swiss gunman shot priest for bothering him.

text.p: A deranged gunman who shot and wounded a priest and a sexton in a Geneva church before surrendering to police on Sunday opened fire because the victims "would not leave me in peace", a Swiss newspaper reported.
Holed up alone in the Notre Dame Roman Catholic Church after the shootings, the gunman called the SonntagsBlick weekly on a mobile telephone as heavily armed police sealed off the area.

"Hello. This is the former head of the city of Basle's military command. I shot a priest and a sexton a few minutes ago because they would not leave me in peace despite my warning," the weekly quoted the man as saying.
"I know I made a mistake. I only wanted to confess my sins to Father Nico. Things have not been going very well for me lately," he added.
The man opened fire with a pistol in the city-centre church shortly after evening mass ended at 7.30 p.m. (1830 GMT) on Saturday, wounding the priest and sexton in the legs.
They escaped with wounds that were not deemed serious.
"The man came into the church and spoke with Father Nico. He was confused and spoke very loudly," a nun who saw the scene unfold told the newspaper.
"As Father Kaufmann wanted to show him out of the church, he drew his pistol and shot him and sexton Giles in the legs."
The gunman demanded to speak with Geneva's police chief, who eventually went into the building and persuaded him to surrender peacefully after a six-hour siege.
Police did not name the 52-year-old man, whom they described as "unbalanced". SonntagsBlick painted a picture of a disturbed individual who threatened violence in the past.
"He is divorced and has had psychological problems for three years," it quoted one of the man's former partners as saying.
"Three weeks ago his circumstances became unberable. He even threatened us physically. We had to cancel the partnership contract with him."
Armed police wearing flak jackets and black masks sealed off the church and cordoned off nearby streets during the siege.
Hundreds of people gathered to watch as policemen crouched along the walls of the church with guns trained on the building.
Police with sniffer dogs moved around the edge of the church, near Geneva's main railway station and the four-star Hotel Cornavin, apparently searching for explosives.
Geneva residents were shocked by the attack, the first they could remember in their normally tranquil city.
"There's a gunman down the road, haven't you heard?," an elderly Swiss lady in a black coat shouted at passers-by in a nearby street.
Switzerland has compulsory military service for men and every able-bodied Swiss male has an assault weapon at home. Switzerland has a 400,000-strong militia army.

Asked if police considered storming the church, gendarmerie officer Fabrizio Tanzi told reporters: "This is not Moscow or Tripoli. This is the international city of Geneva, the city of human rights. We can't go around storming buildings."
